conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What causes the Wernicke–Korsakoff spectrum?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency — classically in chronic alcohol excess, but also in malnutrition, hyperemesis, prolonged vomiting and bariatric surgery.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the relationship between Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Two ends of one disease process — Wernicke's is the acute, reversible phase; Korsakoff's is the chronic, often irreversible amnestic aftermath of untreated/under-treated Wernicke's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the organising principle of the Wernicke–Korsakoff spectrum?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Same deficiency, different stage — Wernicke's is an emergency you can reverse (treat now with parenteral thiamine); Korsakoff's is the permanent memory deficit you were trying to prevent.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the hallmark of Wernicke's encephalopathy vs Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Wernicke's = the classic triad (confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia); Korsakoff's = profound anterograde ± retrograde amnesia with confabulation and apathy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the single most important 'never miss' rule in an at-risk patient?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Give parenteral thiamine BEFORE any glucose/carbohydrate load — a glucose infusion into a thiamine-deplete patient can precipitate Wernicke's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why must Wernicke's be treated empirically on suspicion?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: The full triad appears in only ~10% of cases, so it is a clinical diagnosis treated on any one feature in an at-risk patient.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is Wernicke's encephalopathy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: An acute neurological emergency caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most often in chronic alcohol misuse — reversible if treated promptly, but progressing to irreversible Korsakoff's if untreated.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Confusion + ophthalmoplegia/oculomotor signs (nystagmus, CN VI palsy) + ataxia (broad-based gait).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How common is the complete triad in Wernicke's, and what is the implication?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: It is present in only ~10–16% — so do NOT wait for all three; any one feature in an at-risk patient warrants treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the commonest oculomotor sign in Wernicke's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Nystagmus (also lateral rectus/CN VI palsy and conjugate gaze palsy).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What other features (beyond the triad) can occur in Wernicke's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Hypothermia, hypotension, reduced consciousness/coma, and peripheral neuropathy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why is thiamine essential — the biochemical mechanism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase (pyruvate → acetyl-CoA) and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (Krebs cycle); deficiency impairs glucose oxidation → energy failure in high-demand brain regions.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Which brain regions are damaged in Wernicke's, and what is the memory link?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: The mammillary bodies and medial thalamus (± periaqueductal grey); the mammillary bodies are part of the Papez circuit, so their damage explains the amnesia of Korsakoff's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why is glucose dangerous before thiamine?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Giving glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient consumes the remaining thiamine to metabolise it, precipitating or worsening Wernicke's — so give thiamine before/with glucose (but still treat hypoglycaemia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: List the non-alcohol at-risk groups for Wernicke's.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Malnutrition/starvation and anorexia nervosa, hyperemesis gravidarum, prolonged vomiting, bariatric surgery/malabsorption, refeeding syndrome, dialysis, malignancy and prolonged parenteral nutrition without supplementation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How is Wernicke's diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Clinically — treatment must not wait for tests (a response to thiamine can itself be diagnostic); MRI (mammillary body/thalamic changes) is supportive but negative imaging does not exclude it.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why must magnesium be checked and corrected in Wernicke's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Hypomagnesaemia impairs thiamine's action — thiamine may fail to work unless magnesium is corrected (magnesium is a cofactor).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the Caine criteria for Wernicke's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Dietary deficiency, oculomotor signs, cerebellar signs, and altered mental state — ≥2 of these support the diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the acute treatment of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Immediate IV high-dose thiamine (Pabrinex, parenteral B-vitamins), typically 2–3 pairs TDS for 3–5 days, given before/with glucose; then reducing/oral thiamine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why is thiamine given parenterally (not orally) acutely?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in alcohol misusers, so parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) is needed acutely.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What safety consideration applies to IV Pabrinex?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: There is a small risk of anaphylaxis — give it with resuscitation facilities available.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Who should receive prophylactic thiamine?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: All patients undergoing alcohol withdrawal or otherwise at risk (malnutrition, refeeding risk) — parenteral in higher-risk, oral in lower-risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: A chronic amnestic disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, characterised by profound memory impairment with confabulation — most often the irreversible sequel of untreated Wernicke's encephalopathy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the 'core concept' of Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: It is the chronic, largely irreversible 'memory' end of the thiamine-deficiency spectrum — a selective, dense amnesia in an otherwise relatively intact patient — and it is PREVENTABLE by treating Wernicke's promptly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the triad of clinical features of Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Anterograde amnesia (dominant) + retrograde amnesia + confabulation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the dominant, most disabling feature of Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Anterograde amnesia — an inability to form/acquire NEW memories.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the pattern of retrograde amnesia in Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Loss of memories from before onset, often with a temporal gradient (recent memories lost more than remote ones).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is confabulation, and is it deliberate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: The unconscious filling of memory gaps with fabricated/distorted information — the patient genuinely believes it; it is NOT deliberate lying.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why is Korsakoff's described as a 'selective' amnesia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Memory is devastated, but consciousness, attention, immediate memory and other cognitive domains (and procedural memory) are relatively preserved.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How is Korsakoff's distinguished from delirium?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Korsakoff's has a CLEAR sensorium (clear consciousness, preserved attention), whereas delirium has clouded consciousness, inattention and fluctuation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How is Korsakoff's distinguished from dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Korsakoff's is a SELECTIVE amnesia with other cognition preserved, whereas dementia is a global, progressive cognitive decline.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Which brain structures are damaged in Korsakoff's, and what is the memory link?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: The mammillary bodies and medial/dorsomedial thalamus — the mammillary bodies are a key node of the Papez circuit (hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate), essential for memory consolidation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the biochemical mechanism underlying Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; deficiency causes energy failure in high-demand structures (mammillary bodies, medial thalamus).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What are the causes of Korsakoff's beyond alcohol?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Any cause of thiamine deficiency — malnutrition/starvation, anorexia nervosa, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, prolonged vomiting, malabsorption and refeeding.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How is Korsakoff's diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Clinically — a chronic selective amnestic syndrome with confabulation in a patient at risk of thiamine deficiency (usually after a Wernicke's episode); MRI may show mammillary body atrophy and cognitive testing shows impaired delayed recall with preserved immediate memory/attention.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the overarching management principle for Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: It is largely irreversible → the priority is PREVENTION (treat Wernicke's promptly), plus thiamine replacement, abstinence and supportive care.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the management of established Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Thiamine replacement (still given — modest improvement/halts progression), alcohol abstinence and nutritional support, plus supportive/rehabilitative care, cognitive support and often long-term supervision (many can't live independently).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Should full recovery be expected in Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: No — unlike Wernicke's (reversible), Korsakoff's deficits usually persist; it is largely irreversible.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: A sudden, temporary episode of profound memory loss — predominantly anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) — with other cognitive functions preserved, resolving completely within 24 hours.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What is the 'core concept' defining TGA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Its transience and selectivity — a dramatic but isolated amnesia in an otherwise alert, oriented-to-self, fully-functioning person, that resolves fully; the clinical priority is to distinguish it from dangerous mimics.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: Who typically gets TGA, and what is its prognosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Middle-aged/older adults (50–70); usually a one-off event with an excellent prognosis and low recurrence.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What is the high-yield triad defining TGA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Isolated amnesia + NO focal neurological signs + full recovery within 24 hours.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What is the classic clinical picture of TGA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Sudden anterograde amnesia — the person cannot form new memories, leading to repetitive questioning ('Where am I? What are we doing?') despite being answered.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: Which functions are PRESERVED in TGA (high-yield)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Personal identity (knows who they are), alertness/consciousness, attention, language, and complex/learned tasks (can still drive or cook) — the amnesia is selective.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What is a DEFINING feature of TGA regarding neurology?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: No focal neurological deficit — no weakness, sensory loss, aphasia or visual field defect.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: How long does TGA last, and what is the person left with?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: It resolves completely within 24 hours (usually 4–8h), leaving a permanent gap for the episode itself.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What triggers are associated with TGA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: A trigger shortly before onset — sudden immersion in cold/hot water, physical exertion, emotional stress, Valsalva-type activities (straining, sexual intercourse) or sudden temperature change.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: How is TGA distinguished from TIA/stroke?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: TGA has NO focal neurology; the presence of focal deficits (weakness, aphasia) points to stroke/TIA, which needs urgent assessment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: How is TGA distinguished from transient epileptic amnesia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Transient epileptic amnesia causes brief, recurrent episodes (often on waking) with epileptic features → EEG; TGA is usually a single, longer (up to 24h) episode.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: How is TGA distinguished from dissociative amnesia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Dissociative amnesia often involves loss of personal identity ('who am I?'), whereas in TGA the person KNOWS who they are.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: How is TGA diagnosed and investigated?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Clinically (characteristic syndrome + preserved other functions + resolution); neurological exam must show no focal signs; check glucose (exclude hypoglycaemia), U&E, FBC; imaging/EEG only for atypical/focal/recurrent features.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What are the Hodges and Warlow diagnostic criteria for TGA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: A witnessed attack, anterograde amnesia, no clouding of consciousness or loss of personal identity, no focal neurological/epileptic features, resolution within 24 hours, and no recent head injury/active epilepsy.
Exclude the mimics, then reassure — it is self-limiting with an excellent prognosis and needs no specific treatment; manage vascular risk factors generally.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: How does TGA differ from Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: TGA = transient with full recovery; Korsakoff's = chronic, irreversible amnesia with confabulation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is a substance use disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: A pattern of substance use leading to dependence, harm or impaired control, despite negative consequences.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the 'core concept' framework for substance use disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Identify the substance, then separate the three clinical problems that need different management: (1) intoxication/overdose, (2) withdrawal, and (3) long-term dependence/relapse prevention — the substance × problem grid.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the two high-yield contrasts between alcohol/benzodiazepine and opioid problems?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Alcohol + benzodiazepine WITHDRAWAL is dangerous (seizures, delirium) → needs medically-assisted withdrawal; opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely life-threatening, whereas opioid OVERDOSE is the killer (respiratory depression).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How does alcohol intoxication present, and how is severe alcohol overdose dangerous?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Disinhibition, ataxia and slurred speech; in severe cases coma and respiratory depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How does opioid overdose present, and what is the antidote?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Reduced consciousness, reduced respiratory rate and pinpoint pupils → reversed with naloxone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How does stimulant intoxication present?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Agitation, raised HR/BP, mydriasis (dilated pupils), risk of MI/stroke, and psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the features of dependence (ICD framework)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: A strong desire/compulsion to use (craving), impaired control, tolerance, a withdrawal state on stopping, salience (the substance takes priority), and persistent use despite harm.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the memory anchor for the features of dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Craving · control loss · tolerance · withdrawal · salience · persistence despite harm.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the mechanism of alcohol withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Chronic alcohol enhances GABA and inhibits NMDA/glutamate, so the CNS adapts by downregulating GABA and upregulating NMDA; on stopping, this adaptation is unopposed → CNS hyperexcitability with sympathetic overactivity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why are benzodiazepines the treatment for alcohol withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Because withdrawal is driven by reduced GABA (inhibitory) activity, and benzodiazepines boost GABA, restoring inhibition.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What happens 6–12 hours after the last drink?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Tremor, sweating, tachycardia, anxiety and nausea.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is alcoholic hallucinosis, and when does it occur?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: At ~12–24 hours — classically AUDITORY hallucinations in clear consciousness (visual hallucinations instead suggest delirium tremens).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: When is the peak seizure risk in alcohol withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: At ~36 hours ('rum fits').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: When does delirium tremens occur, and what are its features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: At 48–72 hours — coarse tremor, confusion/delirium, agitation, VISUAL hallucinations, delusions, fever, tachycardia and autonomic instability; a medical emergency with mortality if untreated.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the first-line drug for assisted alcohol withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: A long-acting benzodiazepine — chlordiazepoxide (first-line) or diazepam — in a reducing regimen over ~5–7 days.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which benzodiazepine is preferred for alcohol withdrawal in significant liver impairment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Lorazepam (less accumulation, no active metabolites).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How is delirium tremens managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Benzodiazepines (oral or parenteral; rescue with parenteral lorazepam); haloperidol only as an adjunct for agitation/hallucinations alongside benzodiazepines.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why must thiamine (Pabrinex) always be given in alcohol withdrawal, and when relative to glucose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: To prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy — and it must be given BEFORE glucose (glucose can precipitate Wernicke's in a thiamine-deficient patient).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the three relapse-prevention drugs for alcohol dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Acamprosate, naltrexone and disulfiram (with psychosocial support).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the mechanism and key note for acamprosate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Modulates glutamate/GABA to reduce craving; it is good in hepatic impairment and started after abstinence is achieved.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the mechanism and key caution for naltrexone in alcohol dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: An opioid antagonist that reduces the reward of drinking; avoid in opioid users (precipitates withdrawal) and use with caution in liver disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the mechanism of disulfiram, and its cautions?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase → acetaldehyde builds up → an unpleasant reaction (flushing, vomiting, headache) if alcohol is taken; a deterrent needing a motivated patient — avoid in cardiac disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the classic triad of opioid overdose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Reduced consciousness + reduced respiratory rate + pinpoint pupils (miosis).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the fatal effect in opioid overdose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Respiratory depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the management of opioid overdose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Naloxone (an opioid antagonist), titrated to respiratory function.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why may repeated doses or an infusion of naloxone be needed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Naloxone has a SHORT half-life, so the patient may re-sedate as it wears off (opioids outlast it).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What harm-reduction measure exists for opioid overdose in at-risk patients?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Take-home naloxone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the features of opioid withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Flu-like — agitation, sweating, rhinorrhoea, lacrimation, yawning, DILATED pupils (mydriasis), abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, piloerection and myalgia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the key pupil contrast between opioid overdose and withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Overdose = pinpoint pupils (miosis); withdrawal = dilated pupils (mydriasis).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Is opioid withdrawal dangerous?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: It is very unpleasant (flu-like) but rarely life-threatening — unlike opioid overdose, which is the killer.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is lofexidine, and its role in opioid withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: An α2-agonist used to treat opioid withdrawal symptoms; NICE advises against prescribing opioids purely to manage withdrawal where symptomatic treatment/lofexidine suffices.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What symptomatic treatments are used for opioid withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Lofexidine (α2-agonist) for withdrawal symptoms, loperamide (diarrhoea), antiemetics (nausea) and benzodiazepines (agitation).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What drugs are used for opioid detox/maintenance (substitution)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Methadone (a full agonist; prolongs QTc) OR buprenorphine (a partial agonist).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why must buprenorphine be started once the patient is in withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: As a partial agonist, it can precipitate withdrawal if given too soon after a full agonist, so it is started once the patient is already in withdrawal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is used for relapse prevention after opioid detox?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Naltrexone (an opioid antagonist that blocks the effect of opioids).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What harm-reduction measures apply to opioid dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Needle exchange, blood-borne virus testing (HIV, hepatitis B/C) and vaccination.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Give examples of stimulant drugs of misuse.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Cocaine and amphetamines.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How does stimulant intoxication present?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Agitation, raised HR/BP, mydriasis (dilated pupils), hyperthermia, a risk of MI/stroke/arrhythmia, and stimulant psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Is there a substitution therapy for stimulant dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: No — there is no substitution therapy; management is supportive plus psychological, with benzodiazepines for agitation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How is stimulant intoxication/agitation managed acutely?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Supportively, with benzodiazepines for agitation (and to help the cardiovascular effects).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the key problems with cannabis use?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Dependence and an increased risk of anxiety and psychosis; management is psychological.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why is benzodiazepine dependence significant, and how does its withdrawal compare to alcohol?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Dependence is common, and withdrawal is like alcohol — it can cause seizures and be dangerous.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How is benzodiazepine dependence managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Gradual dose reduction — switch to a long-acting agent (e.g. diazepam), then taper slowly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which two substances share a dangerous, seizure-prone withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Alcohol and benzodiazepines.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What should the history cover in a substance use assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: The substance(s), quantity/frequency, route and duration; features of dependence; previous withdrawal (seizures/DTs); overdose history; injecting and blood-borne virus risk; and the forensic/social context.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which screening tools are used for alcohol?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: CAGE and AUDIT (screening), SADQ (severity of alcohol dependence), and CIWA-Ar (withdrawal severity).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What do the CAGE and AUDIT tools assess?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: They screen for problematic alcohol use/dependence (CAGE is a brief 4-item screen; AUDIT is a fuller alcohol-use screen).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What does the CIWA-Ar score measure, and how is it used?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: The severity of alcohol withdrawal — used to guide symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which bloods are checked in a substance use assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: FBC, U&E, LFTs + GGT, clotting, glucose, and a blood-borne virus screen (HIV, hepatitis B/C).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which blood results suggest chronic alcohol use?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: A raised MCV and a raised GGT.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What should always be screened for alongside a substance use disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Comorbid mental illness and risk — including self-harm/suicide risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What examination findings are looked for in a substance use assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Signs of chronic use and liver disease (and evidence of injecting/blood-borne virus risk).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What are somatisation / medically unexplained symptom disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: A group of disorders where physical symptoms cause distress/impairment but are not fully explained by organic disease, or where the psychological response to symptoms is disproportionate — sitting at the interface of mind and body.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What two questions organise the whole somatisation group?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: (1) Is the patient CONSCIOUSLY producing/feigning the symptoms? and (2) if feigning, is there EXTERNAL gain? These two questions separate every diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: If symptoms are NOT consciously produced, which group of disorders is it?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: The somatoform group — somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder and functional neurological disorder — the patient is genuinely experiencing them and is NOT faking.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: If symptoms are consciously produced and the gain is the sick role, what is the diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Factitious disorder (Munchausen's syndrome) — deliberate feigning for internal/psychological gain (to be a patient).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: If symptoms are consciously produced for external/tangible gain, what is it?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Malingering — deliberate feigning for external reward (money, drugs, time off, avoiding prosecution); NOT a psychiatric diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is the key axis distinguishing factitious disorder from malingering?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Both involve deliberate feigning — they differ only in MOTIVE: factitious = the sick role (internal); malingering = external reward.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What did DSM-5 rename these disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: The 'somatic symptom and related disorders'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is somatic symptom disorder (old name: somatisation disorder)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Multiple real, distressing physical symptoms across systems PLUS disproportionate thoughts/anxiety/behaviour about them, persisting (>6 months; classically ≥2 years without an organic cause).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is illness anxiety disorder (old name: hypochondriasis)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: An excessive preoccupation with HAVING a serious illness (e.g. cancer), despite minimal or no actual symptoms — with 'doctor shopping'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is the high-yield distinction between somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Somatic symptom disorder = distress about REAL symptoms (many, multi-system); illness anxiety disorder = FEAR of having a disease with few/no symptoms ('doctor shopping').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is functional neurological disorder (FND; old name: conversion disorder)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Neurological symptoms (motor/sensory loss, weakness, non-epileptic seizures, blindness) that are incompatible with organic disease, often after a stressor, and NOT consciously produced.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is Hoover's sign, and what does it demonstrate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: A rule-IN sign for functional leg weakness — when the patient lifts the unaffected leg against resistance, you feel involuntary downward pressure (hip extension) in the 'paralysed' leg that was absent on direct testing, showing the motor pathway is intact and the weakness is functional.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is factitious disorder (Munchausen's syndrome)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Deliberately faking or inducing symptoms (e.g. injecting insulin, contaminating samples) for the sick role itself — no external reward.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen's by proxy)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Fabricating or inducing illness in another person (usually a child) — a safeguarding EMERGENCY requiring child protection referral.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: Why should over-investigation be avoided in somatoform disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Repeated tests reinforce illness behaviour and cause iatrogenic harm; the diagnosis should be a POSITIVE one, not endless exclusion.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: Is 'no organic cause found' the same as 'faking'?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: No — the somatoform disorders are genuinely experienced; the diagnosis is positive, not merely one of exclusion, and the patient is NOT faking.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is the overarching management principle for the somatoform group?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: A single, trusted clinician, limited investigation, validation of distress, and treatment of comorbidity — NOT repeated referral/testing.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is the psychological mainstay of treatment for the somatoform disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: CBT (for somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder and FND).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: How is FND specifically managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: A clear positive explanation, physiotherapy (for functional motor symptoms), and MDT input.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is often the highest-yield intervention in somatoform disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Treating comorbid depression/anxiety (e.g. SSRI + psychological therapy) — very common and treatable.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: How is malingering 'managed'?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: It is not treated as an illness — manage the situation (don't provide the sought secondary gain), but consider genuine comorbidity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: How is factitious disorder managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Difficult to manage — avoid confrontation, minimise harm from investigations, and involve psychiatry.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: A transient, temporary inability to move or speak at the transition between sleep and wakefulness — on waking (hypnopompic) or, less often, on falling asleep (hypnagogic).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What is the 'core concept'/mechanism of sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: It is the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep persisting briefly into wakefulness — the mind wakes before the body's REM atonia has switched off, making it benign and self-limiting.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What is the key decisive fork in assessing sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Isolated/benign sleep paralysis (occurs alone, often with sleep deprivation → reassurance) vs sleep paralysis as part of narcolepsy (with excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy and hypnagogic hallucinations → needs sleep studies).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What is the high-yield rule for when to suspect narcolepsy in sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: If it occurs WITH excessive daytime sleepiness + cataplexy + hypnagogic hallucinations, think narcolepsy — sleep paralysis is one of its four cardinal features.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: Why does REM atonia normally exist, and what goes wrong in sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: During REM sleep the skeletal muscles are normally paralysed (atonia) to prevent us acting out dreams; in sleep paralysis this atonia persists briefly into wakefulness, so the person is consciously aware but unable to move.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: How long does sleep paralysis last, and how does it resolve?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Seconds to a couple of minutes; it resolves spontaneously (or when the person is touched or spoken to).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: How is sleep paralysis the 'mirror image' of REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: In RBD the REM atonia is LOST (dreams are acted out); in sleep paralysis the atonia PERSISTS into wakefulness — both are disorders of REM-atonia timing.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What are the core clinical features of sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Transient paralysis of skeletal muscles on waking/falling asleep — conscious but unable to move or speak, with breathing and eye movements preserved and awareness intact.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What hallucinations characteristically occur in sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Vivid, frightening hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations — classically a sense of a threatening presence, pressure on the chest, or a figure (the 'Old Hag' phenomenon).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: Why does intact awareness help distinguish sleep paralysis from other events?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: The person is awake and aware throughout, distinguishing it from a seizure or a faint (syncope).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What are the common triggers/associations of sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Sleep deprivation and irregular sleep schedules (commonest — shift work, jet lag), sleeping supine, stress/anxiety, and narcolepsy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: How is sleep paralysis diagnosed and assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Clinically — a characteristic history of transient paralysis at sleep-wake transitions with intact awareness; the key task is to screen for narcolepsy and refer for sleep studies/MSLT if features are present.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What conditions should be distinguished from sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Seizures, syncope, cataplexy (occurs awake, emotion-triggered), TIA and panic attacks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What is the overarching management principle for sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Reassurance and sleep hygiene for isolated cases; treat any underlying narcolepsy; medication only for frequent/distressing episodes.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What sleep-hygiene measures help sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Adequate, regular sleep; avoiding sleep deprivation; avoiding sleeping supine; reducing stress; and limiting stimulants/alcohol before bed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What medication can be used for frequent/troublesome sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Clonazepam, or a REM-suppressing antidepressant (e.g. an SSRI/TCA), to reduce frequency.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are sleep disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A group of conditions that disrupt the quantity, quality or timing of sleep, or produce abnormal events during sleep — with major impact on mood, cognition and physical health.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the 'core concept' for categorising sleep disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: They sort into a few categories — can't sleep (insomnia), can't stay awake (hypersomnias/narcolepsy), abnormal events (parasomnias), disordered breathing (OSA), abnormal movements (RLS), and mistimed sleep (circadian) — placing the complaint in the right category is the key diagnostic step.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: Match the category to its core complaint: insomnia, hypersomnia, parasomnia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Insomnia = can't fall/stay asleep; hypersomnia = excessive daytime sleepiness despite adequate opportunity (e.g. narcolepsy); parasomnia = abnormal events during sleep (e.g. sleepwalking, night terrors).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: Match the category to its core complaint: sleep-related breathing, movement, circadian.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Sleep-related breathing = snoring + apnoeas + daytime sleepiness (OSA); movement = urge to move/abnormal movements (RLS); circadian = sleep at the wrong time (delayed sleep phase, shift-work, jet lag).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the two main stages of sleep, and their features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Non-REM (N1–N3, including deep slow-wave sleep) and REM sleep (dreaming, with physiological muscle atonia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: From which sleep stage do NON-REM parasomnias arise, and what are their features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Deep slow-wave sleep — occurring early in the night, with NO dream recall, and common in children (e.g. sleepwalking, night terrors).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: From which sleep stage do REM parasomnias arise, and what are their features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: REM sleep — occurring later in the night and dream-related (e.g. nightmares, sleep paralysis, REM sleep behaviour disorder).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How does insomnia relate to psychiatric illness?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: It is frequently comorbid — insomnia both causes and results from mental illness (depression, anxiety, PTSD).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Difficulty falling or staying asleep, with daytime impairment, despite adequate opportunity to sleep.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is chronic insomnia defined?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Symptoms ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months (acute/short-term insomnia is <3 months, often stress-related).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: Which insomnia pattern specifically suggests depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Early-morning waking suggests depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: List the main causes/associations of insomnia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Psychiatric (depression, anxiety), physical (pain, nocturia, respiratory), substances (caffeine, alcohol, stimulants), poor sleep hygiene, and other sleep disorders (OSA, RLS).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is insomnia assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: History plus a sleep diary, bed-partner collateral, screening for depression/anxiety and for OSA/RLS, and a medication/substance review.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia (NICE/CKS)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: CBT for insomnia (CBT-i) — the key modern point is that CBT-i, NOT drugs, is first-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the first steps in managing insomnia before considering drugs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Sleep hygiene and addressing the cause — treat depression/pain, cut caffeine/alcohol, and establish a regular routine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: When and how should a hypnotic be used in insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Only short-term if severe/acute — a z-drug (zopiclone, zolpidem) or short-acting benzodiazepine, at the lowest dose for the shortest time (≤2 weeks), because of dependence, tolerance and falls.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the role of melatonin in insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: An option in adults aged ≥55 (short-term).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is daridorexant, and its role in insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A dual orexin receptor antagonist (NICE TA922) for long-term insomnia where CBT-i has failed or is unavailable.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the overarching prescribing principle in insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Avoid long-term hypnotics — drugs are only a temporary adjunct; CBT-i is first-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A chronic disorder of excessive daytime sleepiness with sudden sleep attacks, caused by loss of orexin (hypocretin) signalling — the wakefulness neuropeptide.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the underlying mechanism of narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Loss of orexin (hypocretin) → intrusion of REM phenomena into wakefulness (cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations are all REM/dream elements breaking through).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the classic tetrad of narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Excessive daytime sleepiness (with sleep attacks), cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the core feature of narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Excessive daytime sleepiness with irresistible sleep attacks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is cataplexy, and why is it significant?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion (e.g. laughter) — highly specific to narcolepsy type 1.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is sleep paralysis in narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A transient paralysis on waking or falling asleep (a REM phenomenon intruding into wakefulness).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are hypnagogic hallucinations?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Vivid hallucinations occurring at sleep onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is narcolepsy diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Sleep studies plus the Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT), and low CSF orexin (hypocretin) levels.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is the excessive daytime sleepiness of narcolepsy managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Sleep hygiene and scheduled naps, plus a stimulant such as modafinil for the sleepiness.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is cataplexy managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: SSRIs/SNRIs or sodium oxybate.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are parasomnias?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Abnormal events occurring during sleep — e.g. sleep paralysis, night terrors, sleepwalking, nightmares and REM sleep behaviour disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is sleep paralysis, and its sleep stage?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A REM-related transient paralysis of skeletal muscles on waking (or falling asleep), ± hallucinations — the normal REM atonia persisting into wakefulness; common and benign.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is sleep paralysis managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Reassurance; clonazepam if troublesome or frequent.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are night terrors, and their sleep stage?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A non-REM (deep sleep) parasomnia — sudden arousal with terror, screaming and an autonomic surge; the child is not fully awake and has no memory; occurs early in the night, in childhood.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is sleepwalking, and its sleep stage?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A non-REM (deep sleep) parasomnia — complex behaviours while asleep, with no memory; occurs in childhood.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are nightmares, and their sleep stage?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A REM parasomnia — frightening dreams WITH recall, occurring later in the night.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A REM parasomnia — loss of the normal REM atonia, causing the person to act out dreams (punching, kicking).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: Why is REM sleep behaviour disorder high-yield?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: It is strongly associated with future α-synucleinopathies (Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies) and often precedes them by years.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How are night terrors distinguished from nightmares?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Night terrors = non-REM, early night, NO recall, child not woken; nightmares = REM, later night, RECALLED.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Repeated upper-airway collapse during sleep → apnoeas/hypopnoeas → repeated arousals → fragmented sleep.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the key clinical features of OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas (reported by a bed-partner), excessive daytime sleepiness, morning headache and poor concentration.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the risk factors for OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Obesity, a large neck circumference, male sex and alcohol.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is OSA assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale to quantify daytime sleepiness, and a sleep study (polysomnography) to confirm the diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the lifestyle measures in OSA management?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Weight loss and avoiding alcohol/sedatives.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the first-line treatment for moderate–severe OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure); mandibular advancement devices are an alternative for milder disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the DVLA implications of OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: The patient must not drive if sleepiness affects driving — OSA with excessive sleepiness must be reported/controlled before driving.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the consequences of untreated OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Hypertension, cardiovascular disease and road-traffic accidents.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is restless legs syndrome (RLS)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: An irresistible urge to move the legs, worse at rest and in the evening, relieved by movement, and disrupting sleep.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the characteristic pattern of RLS symptoms?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Worse at rest/in the evening and relieved by movement — the urge to move the legs improves when the person walks or moves.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the associations of RLS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Iron deficiency (check ferritin — reversible), pregnancy, renal failure and neuropathy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the key reversible cause to check for in RLS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Iron deficiency — check ferritin, as treating it can resolve the symptoms.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is RLS managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Treat iron deficiency, apply sleep hygiene, and use dopamine agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole) or gabapentinoids if severe.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are circadian rhythm sleep disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Disorders where sleep occurs at the wrong TIME, but the sleep itself is normal — e.g. delayed sleep phase (common in adolescents), shift-work disorder and jet lag.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: Give examples of circadian rhythm sleep disorders.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Delayed sleep phase disorder (common in adolescents), shift-work disorder, and jet lag.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How are circadian rhythm disorders managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Sleep scheduling, timed light exposure, and melatonin.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the difference between self-harm and suicide risk?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Self-harm is a BEHAVIOUR (intentional self-injury or self-poisoning, regardless of intent); suicide risk is a clinical ASSESSMENT of the likelihood a person will end their life.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: How do self-harm and suicide overlap?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Self-harm is the single strongest risk factor for later suicide, but most self-harm is NOT a suicide attempt — and many who die by suicide have never self-harmed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the organising principle linking self-harm and suicide assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Every self-harm presentation triggers a suicide-risk assessment, and every risk assessment asks about self-harm — assess the behaviour and the risk together.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Does asking directly about suicide increase risk?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: No — asking directly and sensitively about suicide does NOT increase risk or 'plant the idea'; it is safe, essential, and often brings relief. Always ask.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is self-harm defined as?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Intentional self-poisoning or self-injury, irrespective of the apparent motive — a behaviour, not a diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: By how much does self-harm increase the risk of suicide in the following year?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Around 30–50× increased risk — self-harm is the single strongest risk factor for future suicide.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Which conditions are strongly associated with self-harm?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Depression, borderline PD (EUPD), PTSD, eating disorders and substance misuse.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the single most important/examinable change in NICE NG225 (2022)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: A move AWAY from risk stratification — NICE advises AGAINST using risk-prediction tools/scales and AGAINST 'low/medium/high' stratification to predict risk or to decide who gets treatment or is discharged.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Why does NICE advise against risk-stratification tools?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Risk is dynamic and these tools don't reliably predict individual outcomes; stratifying can wrongly deny care to people labelled 'low-risk'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What replaces risk stratification under NICE NG225?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: A collaborative, compassionate psychosocial assessment producing a risk FORMULATION — a narrative understanding of the person's risks, protective factors and needs, not a category or score.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: If asked 'how do you risk-stratify a self-harm patient?', what is the current correct answer?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: You DON'T stratify into low/medium/high — you undertake a needs-based psychosocial assessment and risk formulation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the status of SAD PERSONS-type mnemonics now?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Worth knowing they exist historically, but they are exactly the risk-scoring tools NICE now advises against relying on for prediction.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Who carries out the psychosocial assessment, and when?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: A mental health professional, at the earliest opportunity — do NOT delay it until medical treatment is completed, and do NOT use intoxication (alcohol) to delay it.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the purpose of the psychosocial assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: To build a collaborative therapeutic relationship, develop a shared understanding of WHY the person self-harmed, identify their needs, and produce a risk formulation — not a stratified score.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What does the psychosocial assessment explore?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: The events/context of the act and mental state; current difficulties and strengths; social circumstances, support and coping resources; mental illness and substance use; and modifiable factors that could increase safety.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the strongest single predictor of future suicide?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Previous self-harm / a previous suicide attempt.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: List demographic and social factors associated with suicide.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Male sex (higher completed suicide), older age (also young adults); unemployment, social isolation, being unmarried/divorced/widowed, bereavement, debt and imprisonment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Why is hopelessness particularly high-yield in suicide assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: It is one of the most significant psychological markers — often MORE predictive than depression severity itself.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What act-related features suggest higher suicidal intent?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: High lethality/planning, precautions against discovery, and a 'final act' such as leaving a note or putting affairs in order.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: List protective factors against suicide.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Strong social support, dependent children, religious/cultural beliefs against suicide, help-seeking, engagement with services, hopefulness/future orientation and reasons for living.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Along what continuum is suicidal ideation explored?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Thoughts (passive 'better off not here' → active thoughts of ending life) → plan → intent → preparation, alongside protective factors.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What does NICE emphasise about HOW ideation is assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: The approach matters more than the checklist — a compassionate, collaborative conversation to understand WHY the person feels this way, rather than mechanically ticking risk items.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the immediate management of a self-harm/overdose presentation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Treat the physical consequences of the act (e.g. paracetamol → N-acetylcysteine; opioids → naloxone; TOXBASE guides specifics), ensure immediate safety, do the psychosocial assessment early, and engage with compassion and without judgement.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the overarching principle of ongoing management (NICE NG225)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Needs-led care — co-produced safety planning, means restriction, and treating the underlying condition — NOT risk-tool-driven disposal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is a safety plan, and what does it include?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: A plan co-produced with the person covering warning signs/triggers, coping strategies, sources of support, means restriction and emergency contacts.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Why is means restriction important?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Reducing access to means is one of the most effective, evidence-based suicide-prevention measures.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the recommended timing of initial aftercare?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment if there are ongoing concerns.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is often the highest-yield intervention in self-harm/suicide management?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Treating the underlying condition (depression, EUPD, PTSD, bipolar, psychosis, substance use).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What psychological interventions are used for self-harm?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Adults — a CBT-based intervention tailored to self-harm; children/young people — consider DBT adapted for adolescents (DBT-A), especially with recurrent self-harm + emotional dysregulation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is 'safer prescribing' for people at risk?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Prescribe medications least dangerous in overdose, in limited quantities, and review access to medicines (prescribed, OTC, herbal) that could be taken in overdose.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What caution applies to antidepressants in under-25s?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Some antidepressants may transiently INCREASE suicidal thoughts in under-25s → arrange closer early review.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: On what basis is admission decided?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: On clinical need and safety — NOT on a risk score; the Mental Health Act is used only if criteria are met and needed care is refused.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: How should borderline PD (EUPD) with recurrent self-harm be managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Respond consistently and compassionately, avoid punitive responses, and manage per the PD approach (DBT; don't medicate the disorder itself).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the correct attitude to repeated self-harm presentations?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Treat each episode on its own merits with the same compassion — never assume 'attention-seeking'; the therapeutic relationship itself affects outcomes and future engagement.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: A loss of contact with reality, defined by POSITIVE symptoms — delusions (fixed false beliefs), hallucinations (perceptions without a stimulus) and thought disorder (disorganised speech/thinking). Psychosis is a symptom/syndrome, not a diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is schizophrenia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: A chronic psychotic disorder with positive + negative symptoms + functional decline, lasting ≥6 months (with ≥1 month of active symptoms) — one cause of psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the organising principle in approaching psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Psychosis is a syndrome with many causes — the diagnostic job is (1) exclude organic and drug causes, then (2) characterise the primary psychiatric disorder using the positive/negative framework and duration.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Describe the epidemiology of schizophrenia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: ~1% lifetime risk; peak onset late teens–20s in men and 20s–30s in women; strong genetic component (highest risk with an affected identical twin).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Why does schizophrenia matter for mortality?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Patients die ~15–20 years early, mostly from cardiovascular disease — so active CVD risk management is essential.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the first and most important split when assessing psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Primary (psychiatric) vs secondary (organic/drug-induced) — always exclude organic and drug causes before diagnosing a primary psychotic disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Give primary psychiatric causes of psychosis.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar/mania, psychotic depression and brief psychotic disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Give secondary (organic/drug) causes of psychosis.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Drugs (stimulants, cannabis, steroids, dopaminergics, withdrawal states) and organic causes (delirium, dementia, temporal lobe epilepsy, encephalitis incl. anti-NMDA, SLE, brain tumour, B12 deficiency).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What clues suggest a SECONDARY (organic/drug) cause of psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Acute onset, older age, clouded/fluctuating consciousness, VISUAL hallucinations, focal neurology, and abnormal observations/bloods.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the high-yield rule about visual hallucinations and consciousness?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Visual hallucinations + clouded consciousness → think organic/delirium, NOT schizophrenia; schizophrenic hallucinations are characteristically auditory with a clear sensorium.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the positive symptoms of schizophrenia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Added experiences — delusions (esp. persecutory, delusions of control), hallucinations (esp. auditory — 3rd-person, running commentary, thought echo), thought disorder, and passivity phenomena.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the negative symptoms of schizophrenia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Lost function — blunted/incongruous affect, anhedonia, alogia (poverty of speech), and avolition (poor motivation) with social withdrawal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the '4 A's' of negative symptoms?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Affect (blunted), Anhedonia, Alogia, and Avolition.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: How do positive and negative symptoms differ in treatment response and impact?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Positive symptoms respond well to antipsychotics; negative symptoms are harder to treat and drive long-term disability.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What features point to schizophrenia over a brief or drug-induced psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Negative symptoms plus a preceding prodrome of social withdrawal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are Schneider's first-rank symptoms (and are they diagnostic)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Auditory hallucinations (3rd-person voices, thought echo, running commentary), thought alienation (insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting), passivity phenomena, and delusional perception — a classic exam framework, NOT diagnostic alone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is delusional perception?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: A normal perception given sudden bizarre delusional meaning (e.g. 'the traffic light turned green, therefore I am the King') — a first-rank symptom.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is thought alienation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Thought insertion, thought withdrawal and thought broadcasting — a first-rank symptom.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Name three other classic schizophrenia features beyond first-rank symptoms.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Catatonia (immobility/bizarre posturing), neologisms (made-up words), and impaired insight.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Define circumstantiality vs tangentiality.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Circumstantiality = excessive detail but eventually answers the question; tangentiality = wanders off and never returns to the point.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the high-yield discriminator between knight's move thinking and flight of ideas?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Knight's move thinking = illogical leaps with NO discernible link (schizophrenia); flight of ideas = rapid leaps WITH discernible links (a manic feature).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Define clang associations and word salad.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Clang associations = words linked by rhyme/sound; word salad = an incoherent string of real words.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Define perseveration and echolalia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Perseveration = repeating ideas/words despite a change of topic; echolalia = repeating others' speech.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Match delusion type to classic disorder: persecutory, grandiose, nihilistic.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Persecutory (being conspired against) = paranoid schizophrenia; grandiose (special powers/identity) = mania; nihilistic (dead/world ended) = psychotic depression (Cotard's).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are delusions of control (passivity) and somatic delusions?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Delusions of control/passivity = thoughts or actions controlled by an external force; somatic delusions = a false belief in a physical/medical problem despite no evidence.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What investigations exclude an organic/drug cause of psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, glucose, calcium, B12/folate), a urine drug screen, CT/MRI head if new-onset/focal/atypical, an autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA) screen if rapid onset with neuro features, and HIV/syphilis serology if indicated.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What baseline tests are needed BEFORE starting antipsychotics, and why?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Weight/BMI/waist, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, ECG (QTc), U&E and LFT — because antipsychotics cause metabolic, QTc and prolactin effects.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: How is schizophrenia diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Clinically (ICD-11/DSM-5) — active symptoms ≥1 month and ≥6 months total; there is no diagnostic test.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the first-line management of a first-episode psychosis (NICE)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: An oral atypical (2nd-generation) antipsychotic (choice guided by side-effect profile) PLUS CBT (offer to all, ≥16 sessions) and family intervention, with referral to an Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) service.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the key antipsychotic prescribing principles?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Trial one antipsychotic at an adequate dose for 4–6 weeks before switching; if inadequate, switch to a second, different antipsychotic; use a long-acting IM depot for poor adherence; and monitor metabolic/prolactin/QTc effects.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What defines treatment-resistant schizophrenia, and what is the treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: An inadequate response to ≥2 adequate antipsychotic trials (at least one an atypical) → clozapine, the most effective antipsychotic for TRS (reserved because of agranulocytosis risk).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the mechanism of antipsychotics, and how does it cause side effects?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Mainly dopamine D2 antagonism — mesolimbic block reduces positive symptoms, but off-target D2 blockade causes side effects (nigrostriatal → EPSEs; tuberoinfundibular → raised prolactin).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Compare typical vs atypical antipsychotics.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Typical (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) — strong D2 antagonism, causing EPSEs + hyperprolactinaemia; atypical (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, clozapine) — D2 + 5-HT2 antagonism, causing metabolic side effects.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Name the four EPSEs with their treatments.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Acute dystonia (torticollis/oculogyric crisis) → procyclidine; akathisia (restlessness) → reduce dose/propranolol; parkinsonism → reduce dose/anticholinergic; tardive dyskinesia (late, choreoathetoid) → tetrabenazine (often irreversible).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Give the key drug-specific antipsychotic points.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Aripiprazole = fewest side effects/least prolactin; haloperidol = QTc prolongation; olanzapine/clozapine = most metabolic/weight gain; all antipsychotics raise stroke/VTE risk and prolactin and can cause NMS.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the key adverse effects and rules for clozapine?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Agranulocytosis/neutropenia (mandatory FBC monitoring), myocarditis (baseline ECG), reduced seizure threshold, constipation (can be fatal ileus), hypersalivation; missed >48h → re-titrate from low dose; smoking cessation raises clozapine levels.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: A life-threatening reaction to dopamine blockade — fever, 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity, autonomic instability and confusion, with markedly raised CK (rhabdomyolysis → AKI) and raised WCC.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: How is NMS managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Stop the antipsychotic, give supportive care with IV fluids and active cooling, and use dantrolene ± bromocriptine in severe cases.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: How is NMS distinguished from serotonin syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: NMS = rigidity + hyporeflexia, onset over days; serotonin syndrome = hyperreflexia/clonus + agitation, rapid onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: List poor prognostic factors in schizophrenia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Insidious (gradual) onset, no clear precipitant, prominent negative symptoms, a prodrome of social withdrawal, low IQ, strong family history, male sex, early onset and poor premorbid functioning.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: List good prognostic factors in schizophrenia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Acute onset, an obvious precipitant, prominent positive (not negative) symptoms, and good premorbid functioning.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: A disorder developing after exposure to a traumatic event (actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence — experienced, witnessed or learned of), characterised by re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal and negative mood/cognition.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is the 'core concept' defining PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: The persistence of a trauma response beyond 1 month — the body stays 'stuck' in threat mode long after the danger has passed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is the decisive timing rule distinguishing PTSD from acute stress disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: <4 weeks of symptoms = acute stress disorder; symptoms persisting >4 weeks (>1 month) = PTSD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: How does adjustment disorder differ from PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Adjustment disorder is a maladaptive response to a NON-catastrophic stressor (divorce, job loss, illness) — low mood/anxiety not meeting full PTSD/depression criteria — arising within ~1 month and resolving within ~6 months.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What are the four symptom clusters of PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal, and negative mood/cognition (emotional numbing) — memory hook: reliving · avoiding · on-edge · numb.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What features make up the RE-EXPERIENCING cluster?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Flashbacks, nightmares, and intrusive distressing images/memories of the event.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What features make up the AVOIDANCE cluster?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Avoiding people, places, situations or reminders of the trauma.
