conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Vomiting loses H⁺ and Cl⁻ (gastric acid), so the loss of hydrogen ions produces a metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Why does recurrent vomiting cause hypokalaemia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Volume loss activates the RAAS → aldosterone retains Na⁺/water and excretes K⁺ in the urine → hypokalaemia; diuretic misuse compounds the potassium loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What ECG changes result from the hypokalaemia of purging?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Flattened T waves and U waves (as in any hypokalaemia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: How does diuretic misuse affect the purging electrolyte picture?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: It compounds the potassium loss, worsening the hypokalaemia already caused by vomiting-induced RAAS activation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: How are eating disorders diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Clinically — from the history, eating behaviour and body-image beliefs, combined with a physical assessment; there is no single diagnostic test.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What must the physical risk assessment in an eating disorder cover?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Weight/BMI trend, observations (bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia), muscle power (sit-up–squat–stand test), bloods and an ECG.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Which bloods are checked in an eating disorder assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: U&E, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, FBC, LFT and TFT.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is looked for on the ECG in an eating disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Bradycardia, a prolonged QTc, and features of hypokalaemia (flattened T waves, U waves).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What comorbidities/risks must be screened for in an eating disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Comorbid depression, anxiety and OCD, plus self-harm/suicide risk and substance misuse.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the SCOFF questionnaire?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: A brief 5-item screening tool for eating disorders (Sick, Control, One stone, Fat, Food); a positive screen prompts referral to a specialist eating disorder service.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the overarching management principle for eating disorders (NICE NG69)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Psychological therapy is the mainstay; medical risk is treated in parallel; and drugs have only a limited role.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line psychological treatment for anorexia nervosa in ADULTS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Individual eating-disorder-focused CBT (CBT-ED), MANTRA (Maudsley Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults), or SSCM (Specialist Supportive Clinical Management).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line psychological treatment for anorexia nervosa in CHILDREN/young people?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-AN); CBT-ED is second-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the role of drugs in anorexia nervosa?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: No drug is first-line for anorexia itself — psychological therapy is the mainstay, with medical risk managed in parallel (electrolytes, refeeding, monitoring) and admission if physical risk is high.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line management of bulimia nervosa in ADULTS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help; if unacceptable or ineffective after ~4 weeks, move to CBT-ED.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line management of bulimia nervosa in CHILDREN/young people?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Family therapy for bulimia (FT-BN); CBT-ED is second-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the drug adjunct in bulimia nervosa?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: An SSRI (fluoxetine) can reduce binge/purge frequency — an adjunct, not the mainstay.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line management of binge eating disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Guided self-help first-line, then CBT-ED if needed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the management of ARFID?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Multidisciplinary dietetic plus psychological management, tailored to the specific driver of restriction.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: When should a patient with anorexia be admitted?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: When physical risk is high (e.g. very low/rapidly falling BMI, dangerous observations, ECG changes or electrolyte disturbance) — to manage refeeding and medical risk safely.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What unites the depressive disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A shared core depressive syndrome — persistent low mood, anhedonia and reduced energy for ≥2 weeks, plus cognitive/biological symptoms — differing mainly in context, timing and trigger, not in the core symptoms.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the organising principle of the depressive disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: The same underlying depression presenting in a different pattern: major depression is the baseline; seasonal affective disorder is depression with a seasonal (usually winter) pattern; postnatal depression is depression with perinatal onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Summarise major depression within the group.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: The core depressive syndrome with no specific temporal pattern; managed with stepped/matched care — psychological options ± an SSRI, and ECT if severe/life-threatening.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Summarise seasonal affective disorder.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Depression with a recurrent seasonal onset (autumn/winter, spring remission), often with atypical features (hypersomnia, increased appetite/carbohydrate craving); treated as depression, with light therapy as an option.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Summarise postnatal depression.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Depression with onset within ~12 months of birth (peak in the early weeks), distinct from transient 'baby blues'; managed with psychological therapy and an SSRI (sertraline if breastfeeding), assessing the mother–infant bond.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What must never be missed in any depressive presentation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Screen for bipolarity (a past manic/hypomanic episode) and assess suicide risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What perinatal distinctions must be made in a depressed new mother?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Distinguish 'baby blues' (self-limiting, <2 weeks) and postpartum psychosis (a psychiatric emergency), and assess the risk to the infant.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Why must you screen for mania/hypomania before starting an antidepressant?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Because an unrecognised bipolar disorder given an antidepressant alone risks precipitating mania.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A mood disorder characterised by persistent low mood, anhedonia and reduced energy, with associated cognitive, biological and functional symptoms, lasting ≥2 weeks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: On what does the diagnosis of depression rest, and what is the key modern management principle?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Three core symptoms + other symptoms + duration (≥2 weeks); and, per NICE, a 'less severe vs more severe' matched-care model in which antidepressants are NOT routinely first-line for less severe depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What conditions must be excluded before diagnosing primary (unipolar) depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Bipolar depression (any past mania/hypomania — changes management entirely), organic/secondary causes (hypothyroidism, anaemia, B12 deficiency, Cushing's, drugs like steroids/β-blockers, substance misuse), pseudodementia in older adults, grief/adjustment, and anxiety disorders.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the three core symptoms of depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Low mood (often worst in the morning — diurnal variation), anhedonia (loss of interest/pleasure) and reduced energy/fatigue.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: List the 'other' symptoms of depression.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Reduced concentration; guilt and worthlessness; appetite/weight change; sleep disturbance (early morning waking); suicidal ideation; psychomotor retardation/agitation; and reduced libido.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: State the ICD severity grades of depression.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Mild = 2 core + 2 other; moderate = 2 core + 3+ other; severe = 3 core + ≥4 other (± psychosis) — all for ≥2 weeks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the biological ('somatic') symptoms of depression, and their significance?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Early morning waking, diurnal mood variation (worse in the morning), appetite/weight loss, reduced libido and psychomotor changes — pointing to more significant depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the validated screening tool for depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: The PHQ-9.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the current NICE (NG222) severity classification, mapped to PHQ-9?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Two categories: 'less severe' (subthreshold + mild, PHQ-9 <16) and 'more severe' (moderate + severe, PHQ-9 ≥16).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What investigations are used in depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Clinical diagnosis (history + mental state exam + PHQ-9); bloods to exclude mimics (TFTs, FBC, U&E, B12/folate, calcium, glucose, LFTs); assess suicide/self-harm risk and screen for bipolarity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the overarching management principle for depression (NICE NG222)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Match treatment to severity + preference; antidepressants are NOT routinely first-line for less severe depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is LESS severe depression (PHQ-9 <16) managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Do NOT routinely offer an antidepressant first-line (only if it is the person's informed preference or has worked before); offer less intrusive psychological/behavioural options (guided self-help, group/individual CBT or behavioural activation, group exercise, mindfulness, IPT, counselling); an SSRI is on the menu but not preferred; active monitoring if treatment is declined.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is MORE severe depression (PHQ-9 ≥16) managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Offer a combination matched to preference — antidepressant + individual CBT is typical first-line, or high-intensity psychological therapy, or an antidepressant alone; the first-line antidepressant is an SSRI.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: When should an antidepressant be reviewed after starting?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: At 2 weeks — or at 1 week if the patient is under 25 or suicidal (higher early suicidal-thought risk).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: For how long should an antidepressant be continued after remission?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: At least 6 months after remission (longer if recurrent) to reduce relapse.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How should antidepressants be stopped?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: By gradual dose reduction (except fluoxetine, which has a long half-life) to avoid discontinuation syndrome.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the first-line antidepressant, in adults and in children/adolescents?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: An SSRI — sertraline in adults; fluoxetine in children/adolescents ('fluoxeTEEN').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the key side effects of SSRIs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: GI upset, GI bleeding (give a PPI if on an NSAID), early anxiety/agitation, hyponatraemia (especially elderly/on diuretics), and sexual dysfunction; citalopram causes QT prolongation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the important SSRI drug interactions?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Warfarin/aspirin (bleeding — avoid co-prescribing), NSAIDs (add a PPI), and triptans/MAOIs (→ serotonin syndrome).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is SSRI discontinuation syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: On abrupt stopping — GI upset, mood change, insomnia, restlessness, sweating, unsteadiness and paraesthesia ('electric shocks') — avoided by tapering (except fluoxetine).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the pregnancy considerations with SSRIs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: 1st trimester → congenital heart defects; 3rd trimester → persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; paroxetine → congenital malformations (avoid); post-MI → sertraline is safest.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the key caution with SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: They are associated with hypertension — check blood pressure before starting and at each titration.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe mirtazapine and its useful niche.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A tetracyclic that blocks α2 receptors → increased noradrenaline/serotonin; it has fewer interactions (good in the elderly/polypharmacy) and its side effects — sedation and increased appetite — make it useful where there is insomnia/poor appetite ('mirtaZapine — zzz + mmm').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe TCAs (amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Not first-line (side-effect burden and overdose danger); more used for neuropathic pain; they block histamine/muscarinic/adrenergic receptors → anticholinergic effects ('can't see, pee, spit, shit'), postural hypotension and QT prolongation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the features of TCA overdose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Confusion, tachycardia, hypotension, mydriasis, a prolonged QRS + QTc, metabolic acidosis and seizures — TCAs are the most dangerous antidepressant class in overdose.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe MAOIs and their key dietary danger.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Phenelzine/tranylcypromine, used for atypical depression (rare); a tyramine ('cheese') reaction — aged cheese/cured meats with an MAOI → a hypertensive crisis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What causes serotonin syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Excess serotonergic activity — e.g. SSRI + MAOI, SSRI + a triptan/tramadol, or overdose.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the triad of serotonin syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity, tremor) + autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating) + altered mental state (agitation, confusion).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is serotonin syndrome managed, and how does it differ from NMS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Stop the serotonergic drug, supportive care and benzodiazepines, with cyproheptadine (a serotonin antagonist) in severe cases; serotonin syndrome has hyperreflexia/clonus with rapid onset, whereas NMS has 'lead-pipe' rigidity + hyporeflexia with slower onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the indications for ECT, and its only absolute contraindication?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Severe, life-threatening or treatment-refractory depression — especially catatonia, refusal of food/fluids, strong suicidal intent, or when a rapid response is needed; the only absolute contraindication is raised intracranial pressure.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the side effects and delivery of ECT?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Headache, nausea, short-term memory impairment, retrograde amnesia (events around treatment) and cardiac arrhythmia; it is given under general anaesthesia + a muscle relaxant, as a course of treatments.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is seasonal affective disorder (SAD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A form of recurrent depression with a seasonal pattern — episodes that reliably occur at a particular time of year (classically winter) and remit at another (spring/summer).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the 'core concept' of SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: It is not a separate disease but depression with a seasonal pattern specifier — diagnosis and management are those of depression, plus the seasonal timing and one SAD-specific option (light therapy).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the distinguishing feature of SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A regular, predictable relationship between mood episodes and the season, present for ≥2 consecutive years.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: State the high-yield rule for diagnosing SAD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: SAD = depressive episodes with a consistent seasonal pattern (≥2 years); the winter pattern is classic (a rarer summer pattern exists), and a single winter of low mood is not enough.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the 'atypical' features of winter SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Hypersomnia (sleeping more, not early-morning waking), hyperphagia with carbohydrate craving → weight gain, and fatigue/leaden heaviness with low energy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How do the symptoms of SAD contrast with typical depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: SAD (atypical) = hypersomnia, hyperphagia and weight gain; typical depression = insomnia (early-morning waking), reduced appetite and weight loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the epidemiology of SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Linked to reduced winter daylight; commoner at higher latitudes and in women.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the pathophysiology of SAD, and its therapeutic rationale?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Reduced winter daylight affects circadian rhythm and melatonin/serotonin regulation (less light → altered melatonin secretion and circadian phase) — the rationale for light therapy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is SAD assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Clinically — a history of recurrent depressive episodes with a seasonal pattern (seasonality over ≥2 years) and PHQ-9 for severity; exclude organic mimics (especially hypothyroidism, which also causes winter fatigue/low mood/weight gain), and screen for suicide risk and comorbidity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the overarching management principle for SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Treat it as depression (per NICE NG222) — psychological therapy and/or an SSRI — with light therapy as a SAD-specific adjunct.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is SAD treated according to severity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Less severe → psychological/behavioural interventions (e.g. CBT) first-line; more severe → an SSRI + psychological therapy (SSRI being the first-line drug).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is light therapy in SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Exposure to a bright light box, particularly in the morning, which can help winter SAD; the evidence is modest/mixed so it is an adjunct/option, but it is the intervention uniquely associated with SAD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the treatment sequence and prophylaxis in SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Psychological therapy → SSRI → light therapy, with lifestyle measures (maximise natural daylight, exercise, regular routine); those with a reliable seasonal pattern may start treatment (light therapy or an antidepressant) before the season begins.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Which drug class should be avoided in SAD, and why?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Sleeping tablets (hypnotics/sedatives) — they worsen the hypersomnia and low energy of SAD and do not treat the disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is postnatal (postpartum) depression (PND)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A depressive episode arising in the postnatal period — meeting the criteria for depression, in the context of new motherhood — distinct from the transient 'baby blues'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the 'perinatal mood triad', and where does PND sit?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Baby blues (mild, transient) → postnatal depression (a true depressive illness) → postpartum psychosis (a psychiatric emergency); PND sits in the middle, and the triad is distinguished by timing and severity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe 'baby blues'.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Onset days 3–10; mild, transient tearfulness, mood lability, irritability and anxiety; resolves spontaneously within ~2 weeks; managed with reassurance and support only (very common, ~50–80%).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe postnatal depression (timing, features, course).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Onset over weeks–months (up to 1 year); a moderate–severe depressive illness with persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, guilt, poor bonding and sleep/appetite change; persistent without treatment (~10–15%).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe postpartum psychosis.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Acute onset (usually within the first ~2 weeks) of psychosis, mania, confusion or severe depression with psychotic features; a psychiatric EMERGENCY, rapidly evolving and dangerous (~1–2/1000), needing urgent admission (Mother & Baby Unit).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the key discriminator across the perinatal mood triad?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Baby blues resolves on its own within ~2 weeks — if low mood persists beyond 2 weeks or is severe, think PND; acute psychosis/mania in the first 2 weeks is postpartum psychosis (an emergency).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Why must perinatal mental illness be actively screened for?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: It is common (~10–20% of women) and a leading cause of maternal death (suicide) in the year after birth — so it must be actively sought and taken seriously.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the perinatal-specific clinical features of PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Core depressive symptoms plus concerns about/difficulty with maternal–infant bonding, guilt about not coping/not being a 'good mother', and anxiety about the baby's health.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What two areas of risk must always be asked about directly in PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Thoughts of self-harm/suicide AND any thoughts of harming the infant — both must be asked about directly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: List risk factors for PND.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A past history of depression/PND or other mental illness, family history, lack of social support, relationship difficulties, an unplanned/complicated pregnancy or birth, and socioeconomic stress; a history of postpartum psychosis or bipolar disorder is a major risk (especially for postpartum psychosis).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the validated screening tool for PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) — a 10-item tool (a score ~≥10–13 prompts further assessment; one item screens for self-harm); the Whooley questions are also used.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What must be excluded when assessing suspected PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Hypothyroidism (postpartum thyroiditis is common and mimics PND — check TFTs), anaemia and other organic causes; also distinguish baby blues (timing/severity) and postpartum psychosis (psychosis/mania — an emergency).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the overarching management principle for PND (NICE CG192)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Treat it as depression matched to severity, with a low threshold for support; choose medication compatible with breastfeeding; and involve the perinatal/health-visiting team — CBT is first-line, with pharmacological treatment added by severity/risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is PND managed by severity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Mild–moderate → psychological therapy first-line (CBT or IPT, guided self-help) with health-visitor/social support; moderate–severe → psychological therapy + an antidepressant; severe/at-risk → specialist perinatal mental health services and consider admission to a Mother & Baby Unit (keeping mother and baby together).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the antidepressant choice in a breastfeeding mother with PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: SSRIs are generally compatible — sertraline (and paroxetine) are favoured (low levels in breast milk); effective treatment should not be withheld for fear of breastfeeding, as untreated PND harms both mother and baby; and psychiatric medication should NOT be stopped abruptly in pregnancy/postpartum (relapse risk) — decide with specialist input.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Summarise postpartum psychosis and its management.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: An acute (usually first 2 weeks) psychosis/mania/confusion or psychotic depression, strongly associated with bipolar disorder/previous postpartum psychosis; a psychiatric emergency needing urgent assessment and admission (Mother & Baby Unit), treated with antipsychotics/mood stabilisers ± ECT.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: An acquired, chronic, usually progressive decline in cognition (memory, language, executive function, personality) severe enough to impair daily function, occurring in clear consciousness.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the three-step framework for approaching dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: (1) Is it dementia at all, or a mimic (delirium, depression)? → (2) which subtype? → (3) manage cognition + BPSD + risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Why do the mimics of dementia matter most?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Because delirium and depression are reversible and must not be mislabelled as dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is BPSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia — agitation, psychosis, depression and sleep disturbance.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Contrast the onset/course of dementia, delirium and depression (pseudodementia).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Dementia = insidious (months–years), progressive, stable day-to-day; delirium = acute (hours–days), fluctuating (worse at night); depression = subacute (weeks), relatively stable.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Contrast consciousness/attention and memory in dementia vs delirium vs depression.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Dementia = clear consciousness (attention preserved early), early memory loss with the patient often unconcerned; delirium = clouded/inattentive (the hallmark), poor registration; depression = clear consciousness, 'don't know' answers with the patient worried.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: State the three pattern rules for dementia vs its mimics.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Acute + fluctuating + inattentive + clouded → delirium (exclude first); short history + biological symptoms + patient distressed about memory + 'don't know' answers + global loss → depression (pseudodementia); insidious + progressive + clear consciousness + patient unconcerned → dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Give the one-line discriminators for the four main dementia subtypes.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Alzheimer's = memory first, gradual; vascular = stepwise + vascular risk factors + focal neurology; DLB = fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism; FTD = personality/language change first with memory spared early (younger, <65).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the commonest dementia, and its underlying pathology?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Alzheimer's disease (~60%) — insidious, gradual, early memory loss; pathology is amyloid-β plaques + tau neurofibrillary tangles with a cholinergic (↓ACh) deficit.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the pathology of the non-Alzheimer's dementia subtypes?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Vascular = cerebrovascular disease (stepwise); DLB = α-synuclein (Lewy bodies); frontotemporal dementia = tau (Pick bodies)/TDP-43.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the clinical hallmark of Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Early, prominent memory loss (recent memories lost first), gradually progressing to global cognitive decline; it is the commonest dementia (~60%).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What are the '4 A's' of Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Amnesia (recent memories lost first), Aphasia (word-finding difficulty, muddled/disjointed speech), Agnosia (recognition problems — faces, objects) and Apraxia (inability to carry out skilled tasks despite normal motor function).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is amnesia in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Loss of memory, with recent memories lost first.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is aphasia in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Word-finding difficulty with muddled/disjointed speech.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is agnosia in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Difficulty recognising things — faces and objects.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is apraxia in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: An inability to carry out skilled tasks despite normal motor function.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the pathology of Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Extracellular amyloid-β plaques and intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the neurotransmitter deficit in Alzheimer's, and its therapeutic rationale?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: A cholinergic deficit (reduced acetylcholine) — the rationale for acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: How does the onset/course of Alzheimer's distinguish it from the other subtypes?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Alzheimer's is insidious and gradual with memory affected first — versus vascular (stepwise + vascular risk), DLB (fluctuating + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism) and FTD (personality/language first, memory spared early).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine (boosting acetylcholine to counter the cholinergic deficit).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the role of memantine in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: An NMDA-receptor antagonist used for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's (or added to an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, or if an AChE inhibitor is not tolerated/contraindicated).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Which conditions/factors increase the risk of Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Increasing age, family history, Down syndrome (an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21), the ApoE4 allele, and vascular risk factors.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Cognitive impairment caused by cerebrovascular disease — the second commonest dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the characteristic progression of vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Classically a stepwise progression — each 'step' represents a further vascular insult — often with focal neurology.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Why is the decline in vascular dementia 'stepwise' rather than gradual?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Because each new vascular insult (stroke/infarct) causes a further, discrete drop in cognition, producing a stepwise rather than a smooth gradual decline.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What vascular risk factors are associated with vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation and smoking.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What are the subtypes of vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Post-stroke dementia, subcortical small-vessel dementia, and mixed dementia (coexisting with Alzheimer's — common).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is mixed dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Coexisting vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease — a common combination.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: How does vascular dementia differ from Alzheimer's disease clinically?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Vascular = stepwise decline with focal neurology and vascular risk factors; Alzheimer's = gradual, insidious decline with early prominent memory loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Why is focal neurology a clue to vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Because the underlying strokes/infarcts damage discrete brain regions, producing focal neurological signs — unlike the diffuse, gradual picture of pure Alzheimer's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the management emphasis in vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Controlling cardiovascular risk factors (the modifiable part) to slow progression, symptomatic treatment, and advance care planning.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Are cognitive-enhancing drugs (AChE inhibitors/memantine) routinely used in pure vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: No — they are not routinely used for pure vascular dementia; they are considered only if there is suspected comorbid Alzheimer's, DLB or Parkinson's disease dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is post-stroke dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Cognitive impairment/dementia that follows a stroke, part of the vascular dementia spectrum.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is subcortical vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Vascular dementia from small-vessel disease affecting the subcortical white matter.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the core triad of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Fluctuating cognition + recurrent visual hallucinations + spontaneous parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Describe the cognitive feature of DLB.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Fluctuating cognition — attention and alertness vary markedly, often over hours or days.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Describe the hallucinations of DLB.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Recurrent, typically well-formed visual hallucinations.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What parkinsonian features occur in DLB?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Spontaneous parkinsonism — bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What additional (non-triad) features occur in DLB?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams — often preceding it by years), autonomic dysfunction, and repeated falls.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the significance of REM sleep behaviour disorder in DLB?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: It (acting out dreams) often precedes DLB by years and is an early marker.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the pathology of DLB?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: α-synuclein deposition (Lewy bodies) — the same protein as in Parkinson's disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: How does DLB relate pathologically to Parkinson's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Both are α-synuclein (Lewy body) disorders; they are distinguished by the timing of dementia relative to parkinsonism.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: State the '1-year rule' distinguishing DLB from Parkinson's disease dementia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Dementia before, or within 1 year of, the onset of parkinsonism → DLB; parkinsonism preceding dementia by >1 year → Parkinson's disease dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the critical drug sensitivity in DLB?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Antipsychotic sensitivity — people with DLB can have severe, sometimes fatal reactions to antipsychotics (worsening parkinsonism, sedation, NMS-like reactions), so antipsychotics are avoided if at all possible.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: If an antipsychotic is unavoidable in DLB, how should it be used?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: At the lowest dose of an atypical antipsychotic, with extreme caution.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: How is DLB distinguished from Alzheimer's disease clinically?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: DLB = fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism (± REM sleep behaviour disorder, falls); Alzheimer's = gradual, insidious decline with early prominent memory loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is frontotemporal dementia (FTD/Pick's disease)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: A dementia characterised by early personality and behaviour change and/or language impairment, with memory relatively preserved early — the key contrast with Alzheimer's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What behavioural features characterise FTD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and compulsive behaviours.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What language feature can characterise FTD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Language impairment — a progressive aphasia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the key contrast between FTD and Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: In FTD, personality/behaviour and/or language change first, with memory relatively preserved early; in Alzheimer's, memory is affected early and prominently.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the typical age of onset of FTD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Younger onset, often before 65.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the pathology of FTD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Pick bodies (accumulation of tau protein within neurones) and/or TDP-43.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the key management point in FTD regarding cognitive-enhancing drugs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Do NOT give acetylcholinesterase inhibitors or memantine in FTD — they are of no benefit and may worsen it.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Why are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors not used in FTD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: FTD does not have the cholinergic deficit that underlies Alzheimer's, so these drugs offer no benefit and may worsen the condition.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the behavioural variant of FTD dominated by?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Early personality/behaviour change — disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and compulsive behaviours.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the language-led presentation of FTD called?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Primary progressive aphasia (a progressive language impairment).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: How does FTD differ from DLB and vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: FTD = younger, personality/language change first with memory spared early (Pick/tau/TDP-43). DLB = fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism (α-synuclein). Vascular = stepwise decline + focal neurology + vascular risk factors.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What cognitive assessment tools are used in dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Bedside screening tools — MMSE, MoCA, 6-CIT, AMTS — with formal neuropsychology if needed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Which blood tests are essential to exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs (hypothyroidism), calcium, glucose/HbA1c, and B12 + folate; plus HIV/syphilis serology if indicated.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Why is a medication review important in dementia assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Because a high anticholinergic burden worsens cognition — such drugs should be identified and reduced.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the role of neuroimaging in dementia, and which modality is preferred?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: MRI (preferred) to exclude structural causes (tumour, subdural haematoma, normal pressure hydrocephalus) and to assess atrophy/vascular load.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What imaging supports a diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: A DAT scan showing reduced dopamine transporter uptake.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Why is a depression screen part of the dementia work-up?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: To exclude depression (pseudodementia), a reversible mimic.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the overarching management principle in dementia (NICE NG97)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Subtype-specific cognitive drugs + non-drug-first management of BPSD + support, advance care planning and cardiovascular risk control.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the drug management of Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: First-line for mild–moderate disease: an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine); memantine (an NMDA antagonist) for severe disease, or for moderate disease if an AChE inhibitor is not tolerated, or as an add-on.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the drug management of dementia with Lewy bodies?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil/rivastigmine) — often effective (marked cholinergic deficit); memantine if these are not tolerated.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the drug management of vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Control cardiovascular risk factors; AChE inhibitors/memantine only if a comorbid Alzheimer's, DLB or Parkinson's disease dementia is suspected.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the drug management of frontotemporal dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Do NOT use acetylcholinesterase inhibitors or memantine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What cardiac cautions apply to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: They are pro-cholinergic, so avoid/use caution with QT prolongation, bradycardia and cardiac conduction problems (they can cause bradycardia); where QT is prolonged, use cognitive stimulation therapy instead. Re-titrate rivastigmine/galantamine if >3 days are missed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the first-line approach to BPSD (behavioural & psychological symptoms of dementia)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Non-pharmacological measures first — identify triggers (pain, infection, constipation, environment), person-centred approaches, cognitive stimulation and structured activity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: When and how are antipsychotics used for BPSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Only if there is severe distress or risk to self/others AND non-drug measures have failed — short-term, at the lowest dose (e.g. risperidone).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What are the risks of antipsychotics in elderly dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Increased stroke and increased mortality — so they are used sparingly and reviewed regularly; in DLB they are avoided altogether (severe antipsychotic sensitivity).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What supportive measures apply across all dementias?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Psychoeducation and carer support, occupational therapy and a structured routine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What legal/planning and safety measures apply in dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Advance care planning, Lasting Power of Attorney, capacity assessments, treating comorbid depression, DVLA notification, and safeguarding.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Why is it essential to exclude reversible causes before diagnosing dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: To avoid mislabelling a treatable condition (e.g. hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, normal pressure hydrocephalus, subdural haematoma, depression) as irreversible dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is cognitive stimulation therapy, and when is it particularly used?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: A non-drug cognitive intervention; it is used, for example, where an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is contraindicated (e.g. QT prolongation).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Summarise the subtype-specific drug approach across dementias.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Alzheimer's → AChE inhibitor (memantine for severe); DLB → AChE inhibitor (avoid antipsychotics); vascular → cardiovascular risk control (cognitive drugs only if comorbid AD/DLB/PD dementia); FTD → no AChE inhibitor/memantine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What defines the delusional & misidentification syndromes?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: A group of disorders defined by specific, characteristic delusions — fixed false beliefs held despite contradictory evidence — several with classic eponymous names (Capgras, Cotard, Othello…).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What is the 'core concept' for organising these syndromes?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Organise by what the delusion is about — misidentification (people/identity), content themes (jealousy, love, death, infestation), or isolated delusional disorder — and always identify the delusion type AND find its cause (each can be primary or secondary).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: Contrast primary and secondary delusional syndromes.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Primary = a primary psychotic/delusional disorder; secondary = organic (dementia — especially Lewy body — delirium, brain lesion, epilepsy) or another psychiatric disorder (schizophrenia, mood disorder with psychosis).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What clues suggest a secondary (especially organic) cause of a delusional syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Older age, cognitive impairment, acute onset, fluctuation, focal signs, or a mood episode.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: Which delusional syndromes are especially likely to be organic, and which is classically from psychotic depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: The misidentification syndromes (Capgras, Fregoli) are frequently secondary to organic disease (dementia, especially Lewy body) as well as schizophrenia — always consider an organic cause, particularly in older patients; Cotard's is classically secondary to severe (psychotic) depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: List the delusion types by content and their classic associations (part 1).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Persecutory (being conspired against/harmed — paranoid schizophrenia); grandiose (special powers/status — mania); nihilistic (self/body/world dead or non-existent — psychotic depression → Cotard's).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: List the delusion types by content and their classic associations (part 2).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Control/passivity (thoughts/actions controlled externally — schizophrenia); somatic (a physical/medical problem despite no evidence — delusional disorder); reference (ordinary events have special personal meaning — schizophrenia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What is the Capgras delusion?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: The belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor ('clone/double') — memory hook 'Capgras = Clone'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What is Fregoli syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: The belief that strangers are actually a familiar person in disguise (or that everyone is the same person in disguise) — 'Fregoli = Familiar in disguise', the mirror image of Capgras.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: Contrast Capgras and Fregoli.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Capgras = a familiar person seen as a stranger/impostor ('you're not really my husband'); Fregoli = strangers seen as a familiar person in disguise ('that stranger is really my husband in disguise') — mirror images; both are frequently associated with organic disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What is Cotard syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: The belief that oneself (or a body part) is dead, non-existent, or rotting — a nihilistic delusion associated with severe (psychotic) depression and psychotic disorders.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What is Othello syndrome, and its key risk?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Pathological jealousy — a fixed belief that the partner is being unfaithful; it may be isolated or secondary (affective disorder, schizophrenia, personality disorder, alcohol misuse) and carries a significant risk of violence/harm to the partner (a forensic-risk delusion).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What is De Clérambault syndrome (erotomania)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: The belief that another person (often of higher status) is secretly in love with them, receiving 'secret messages' from the 'admirer'; it can lead to stalking/harassment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What is delusional parasitosis (Ekbom syndrome)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: A fixed belief of being infested with bugs/parasites, with excoriations from scratching and the 'matchbox sign' (bringing 'specimens'); it may be primary or organic/drug-induced.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What is Charles-Bonnet syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Complex visual hallucinations in people with significant visual impairment/eye disease (e.g. macular degeneration, glaucoma), occurring in clear consciousness and WITH insight — typically faces, children and animals, which the person usually knows are not real.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: Why is Charles-Bonnet syndrome NOT a psychosis, and how is it managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: It is a release phenomenon of visual loss (insight retained, no other psychotic features), so it must not be misdiagnosed as a psychotic disorder; management is reassurance plus optimising vision/treating the eye disease (not antipsychotics).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: How are the delusional syndromes assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Clinically — characterise the delusion (content, conviction, fixity), assess insight and do a full mental state exam; always look for an underlying cause (psychiatric or organic — consider cognitive assessment + neuroimaging, especially in misidentification syndromes and older patients); and assess risk (Othello — violence; erotomania — stalking).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: What is the overarching management principle for these syndromes?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Treat the underlying condition, use antipsychotics for the delusion, and address risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: How is management directed by the underlying cause?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Antidepressants (± antipsychotics/ECT) for Cotard's (psychotic depression); antipsychotics for schizophrenia-related delusions and delusional disorder; treat any organic cause (with caution about antipsychotics in Lewy body dementia); and reassurance + optimising vision for Charles-Bonnet (not antipsychotics).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: How is risk managed in Othello syndrome and erotomania?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Othello syndrome — assess/manage the risk of violence to the partner (may need separation/safeguarding); erotomania — manage the stalking/harassment risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: How is delusional parasitosis managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Treat the underlying cause, use antipsychotics, and arrange dermatology + psychiatry liaison.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.front: Why must an organic cause always be considered in a misidentification syndrome, especially in the elderly?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.back: Because Capgras and Fregoli are frequently secondary to organic disease (dementia, especially Lewy body, and neurological lesions) — so cognitive assessment and neuroimaging should be considered.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is bipolar affective disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: A chronic mood disorder defined by episodes of mania/hypomania alternating with depression, with periods of normal (euthymic) mood between.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is the 'core concept' separating bipolar from unipolar depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: The presence of at least one manic or hypomanic episode — so the single most important question is 'has there ever been a high?'

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: Describe the epidemiology of bipolar disorder.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Onset typically in the late teens–20s, a strong genetic component, and a high suicide risk (~15× the general population).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What features are shared by mania and hypomania?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Both involve abnormally elevated or irritable mood with increased energy, reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, distractibility and disinhibition/risk-taking; they differ in severity, duration and psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: Define mania.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Elevated/irritable mood lasting ≥7 days with severe functional impairment (disrupting work/social function), possibly needing hospitalisation, and with psychotic symptoms (grandiose delusions, hallucinations) able to occur.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: Define hypomania.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Elevated/irritable mood lasting <7 days (≥4 days) with mild impairment (function largely preserved), hospitalisation unlikely, and NEVER psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is the high-yield rule distinguishing mania from hypomania?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Psychosis OR marked impairment/hospitalisation = mania; milder, no psychosis, function preserved = hypomania — psychotic features automatically make it mania.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: Contrast bipolar I and bipolar II.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Bipolar I = mania (± depression) — mania alone diagnoses it, depression not required. Bipolar II = hypomania + depression (never full mania) — requires both.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: If a patient has ever had a true manic episode, which type do they have?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Bipolar I.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is cyclothymia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: A milder, chronic mood fluctuation (subthreshold highs and lows) that does not meet the full criteria for bipolar disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What are the mood and cognitive features of a manic episode?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Elevated/euphoric or irritable mood, flight of ideas (rapid speech leaping between topics with discernible links), grandiosity/grandiose delusions, distractibility and poor insight.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What are the behavioural features of a manic episode?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Reduced need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, disinhibition, pressured/rapid speech, and reckless behaviour (overspending, risky sex, impulsive decisions); severe episodes include psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: Contrast flight of ideas with knight's move thinking.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Flight of ideas (leaps between topics with discernible links) is the manic thought disorder; knight's move thinking (leaps with NO links) occurs in schizophrenia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What investigations exclude secondary causes of a manic presentation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Bloods (TFTs for hyperthyroidism, U&E, LFTs, glucose, calcium), a urine drug screen (stimulants), and imaging if atypical/focal signs; also exclude steroid-induced mania and substance use.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What baseline investigations are needed before starting mood stabilisers?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Lithium → U&E + eGFR, TFTs, calcium (kidney/thyroid/parathyroid effects); valproate → LFTs + FBC; antipsychotics → weight/BMI, glucose, lipids, ECG; and a pregnancy test/contraception (valproate and lithium are teratogenic).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: How is bipolar disorder diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Clinically — a collateral history is invaluable, as patients often lack insight into their highs.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is the overarching management principle in bipolar disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Treat the acute episode → maintain long-term prophylaxis → and watch antidepressants (which can trigger mania).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: How is acute mania/hypomania managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: If not on treatment → an antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone or haloperidol) first-line; if already on treatment → optimise/add; STOP any antidepressant (it may be driving the mania); with agitation → IM antipsychotic ± a benzodiazepine, without → oral antipsychotic monotherapy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: How is acute bipolar depression managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Do NOT use an antidepressant alone (risk of switching to mania); options include quetiapine, olanzapine (± fluoxetine) or lamotrigine, plus CBT — the highest switch risk is with venlafaxine/TCAs.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is the first-line long-term prophylaxis in bipolar disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Lithium — the most effective mood stabiliser, which also reduces suicide risk; if ineffective/not tolerated → valproate (2nd-line) or an antipsychotic (e.g. quetiapine), ± combining.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is the current restriction on prescribing valproate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Do NOT start valproate in anyone (male or female) under 55 unless two specialists independently document there is no alternative (teratogenicity and fertility/testicular effects); never in women of childbearing potential without a pregnancy prevention programme.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What psychosocial measures and referral thresholds apply in bipolar disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Psychoeducation, CBT, mood monitoring, sleep/routine regulation and addressing substance use; CMHT referral — routine if hypomania, urgent if mania or severe depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is the use and mechanism of lithium?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Bipolar prophylaxis (first-line) and augmentation in refractory depression; it also reduces suicide risk; it interferes with cAMP and inositol-triphosphate second-messenger signalling and has a narrow therapeutic index.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: List the side effects of lithium (LITHIUM mnemonic).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Lethargy; Insipidus (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus → polyuria); Tremor (fine); Hypothyroidism; Insides (GI — nausea, diarrhoea); Urine ↑; Metallic taste — plus weight gain, nephrotoxicity, hyperparathyroidism → hypercalcaemia, benign leucocytosis and T-wave flattening/inversion.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What precipitates lithium toxicity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Dehydration, illness, renal impairment and drug interactions (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides) — all of which reduce lithium clearance.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What are the features and management of lithium toxicity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: A coarse tremor (vs the fine tremor at therapeutic levels), ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, nystagmus, seizures, arrhythmias and visual disturbance — often GI symptoms first then neurological. Management: stop lithium, IV fluids (rehydrate → increase excretion), correct electrolytes, control seizures, and haemodialysis if severe.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: How is lithium monitored?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Levels are taken 12 hours post-dose; weekly after starting/dose change until stable, then every 3 months; TFTs and renal function (U&E/eGFR) every 6 months, plus calcium.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is the use and mechanism of valproate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Bipolar disorder (2nd-line prophylaxis and acute mania — subject to the <55 restriction); it blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and is a CYP enzyme inhibitor.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: List the side effects of valproate (VALPROATE mnemonic).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Vomiting; Alopecia; Liver toxicity; Pancreatitis/Pancytopenia; Retention of fat (weight gain); Oedema; Anorexia; Tremor; Enzyme inhibition — and it is TERATOGENIC (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental effects), the reason for the strict prescribing restriction.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: What is the role and side-effect profile of antipsychotics in bipolar disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Used for acute mania, bipolar depression (quetiapine, olanzapine) and prophylaxis; the same side-effect profile as in schizophrenia — EPSEs, metabolic effects, hyperprolactinaemia and NMS.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.front: Which antidepressant carries the highest risk of triggering a switch to mania in bipolar disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.back: Venlafaxine (also TCAs) — antidepressants can trigger mania, so antidepressant monotherapy is avoided in bipolar depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What unites the anxiety & stress-related disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: A group united by pathological anxiety, fear or a stress response that is out of proportion, persistent and impairs function; they are separated by what drives the anxiety and its time course.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is the organising principle for the anxiety disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Pin down the pattern: GAD = generalised uncontrollable worry; panic disorder = recurrent unexpected panic attacks + anticipatory fear; OCD = obsessions driving compulsions; acute stress reaction = transient symptoms right after an exceptional stressor.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Summarise generalised anxiety disorder (GAD).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Excessive, uncontrollable worry across multiple domains plus restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, muscle tension and sleep disturbance, most days for ≥6 months; first-line is stepped care with CBT and/or an SSRI (sertraline).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Summarise panic disorder.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks with persistent worry about further attacks/avoidance; recurrent and episodic; first-line CBT, with an SSRI.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Summarise OCD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Obsessions (intrusive thoughts) driving compulsions (rituals) — distressing and time-consuming; chronic and fluctuating; first-line CBT with ERP (exposure & response prevention), with an SSRI (often higher dose).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Summarise acute stress reaction.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Marked anxiety/dissociative symptoms after an exceptional stressor, with onset within minutes–hours that resolves within days (<1 month); managed with reassurance and supportive care, watching for progression to PTSD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What are the two key distinctions to remember across the anxiety spectrum?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Acute stress reaction resolving in days ≠ PTSD (symptoms persisting >1 month, a separate topic); and OCD's specific therapy is ERP, not generic CBT alone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What must be done in every suspected anxiety disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Screen for comorbid depression, substance use and suicide risk, and exclude organic mimics (e.g. hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, caffeine/stimulants) before settling on a primary anxiety diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Persistent, excessive, generalised worry about a range of everyday events/activities, present 'more days than not', with physical and psychological symptoms of anxiety causing distress/impairment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is the 'core concept' of GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: It is free-floating, pervasive worry not tied to a specific object or situation — distinguishing it from panic disorder (discrete attacks), phobias (specific triggers) and OCD (obsessions/compulsions); organic and drug causes must be excluded first.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Which secondary (organic/drug) causes must be excluded before diagnosing GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Hyperthyroidism (tremor, weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance → check TFTs), cardiac arrhythmia (e.g. SVT)/phaeochromocytoma, drug/substance-induced (salbutamol, theophylline, corticosteroids, caffeine, early antidepressants, stimulants; alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal), and other psychiatric disorders.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is the high-yield rule before diagnosing primary GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Always exclude hyperthyroidism, cardiac disease and drug/caffeine causes first.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: How is GAD distinguished from panic disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: GAD = constant, pervasive worry — anxious most of the time (often can't identify a single worry); panic disorder = short bursts of intense fear with well periods between episodes ('fear of fear').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: How is GAD distinguished from phobias, OCD and PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Phobias = anxiety triggered by a specific object/situation; OCD = obsessions + compulsions; PTSD = anxiety following trauma with re-experiencing/avoidance; GAD = generalised, free-floating worry.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What are the psychological features of GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Excessive, uncontrollable worry; restlessness/being 'on edge'/apprehension; poor concentration/mind going blank; irritability; and sleep disturbance.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What are the physical (autonomic) features of GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Palpitations/tachycardia, tremor/sweating, GI upset/dry mouth, muscle tension/headache, fatigue/dizziness and a 'lump in the throat'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is the duration criterion for GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Worry present more days than not for ≥6 months.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What screening/severity tool is used in GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: The GAD-7 questionnaire (higher scores = more severe).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: List risk factors for GAD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Age 35–54, being divorced/separated, living alone, being a lone parent, female sex, family history, childhood adversity and comorbid physical illness.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Explain the hyperventilation → hypocalcaemia physiology of a panic attack.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Panic → hyperventilation → blowing off CO₂ → low arterial CO₂ → respiratory alkalosis (raised pH); the alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin → reduced ionised (free) calcium → functional hypocalcaemia → peri-oral and peripheral tingling/paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What investigations are used in suspected GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Clinical diagnosis (history + GAD-7); bloods to exclude mimics — TFTs (hyperthyroidism), FBC, glucose; ECG if palpitations/cardiac concern; review medications and caffeine/alcohol/substance use; and screen for comorbid depression and suicide risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is the overarching management principle for GAD (NICE CG113)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Stepped care — education/monitoring → low-intensity psychological → high-intensity psychological OR drug treatment → specialist; SSRIs are first-line drugs and benzodiazepines are NOT used for GAD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Outline steps 1 and 2 of the GAD stepped-care model.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Step 1 = identification, education and active monitoring (may resolve milder cases); Step 2 = low-intensity psychological interventions — guided self-help (CBT-based) and psychoeducational groups.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Outline steps 3 and 4 of the GAD stepped-care model.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Step 3 = high-intensity psychological therapy (CBT or applied relaxation) OR drug treatment (patient choice); Step 4 = specialist referral for severe cases, marked impairment, high risk or significant comorbidity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is the drug treatment ladder for GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: First-line: an SSRI (sertraline — most cost-effective, off-label). If ineffective: an alternative SSRI or an SNRI (venlafaxine/duloxetine), minding withdrawal (worst with paroxetine/venlafaxine) and overdose toxicity (venlafaxine). If not tolerated: pregabalin (third-line — a controlled drug, dependence/misuse risk, caution in pregnancy).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What should be avoided, and what adjuncts are used, in GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Do NOT offer a benzodiazepine (except short-term crisis) or an antipsychotic (in primary care); propranolol helps autonomic symptoms (tremor, palpitations) only and doesn't treat the worry; buspirone is an option but not first-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What monitoring and treatment duration apply in GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Review early (especially those <25 or at suicide risk) and continue effective treatment for ≥1 year (high relapse risk).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is panic disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Recurrent, unexpected panic attacks (discrete episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms) plus persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive change in behaviour because of them.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is the 'core concept' of panic disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: The defining feature is the discrete, sudden panic attack peaking within minutes, and the disorder is perpetuated by the 'fear of fear' cycle — distinguishing it from GAD's constant background worry; it is often misinterpreted as a heart attack (repeated A&E/cardiology presentations).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Distinguish a panic attack from panic disorder.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: A panic attack is a symptom (a discrete surge of intense anxiety) that can occur in many conditions; panic disorder is recurrent UNEXPECTED (unprovoked) panic attacks plus persistent anticipatory worry — the attacks come 'out of the blue'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Which organic mimics must be excluded in suspected panic disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Cardiac arrhythmia (SVT)/ACS (chest pain, exertional → ECG), hyperthyroidism (tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance → TFTs), phaeochromocytoma (episodic ↑BP + headache + sweating), hypoglycaemia (in diabetics; relieved by glucose), substances (stimulants, caffeine, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal) and respiratory causes (asthma, PE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: What is the rule about investigating panic disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: It is a diagnosis after excluding organic causes (especially cardiac, thyroid, substance), but avoid over-investigating once the pattern is clear, as this reinforces health anxiety.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Describe a panic attack.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: A discrete episode of intense fear peaking within ~10 minutes, with ≥4 symptoms.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: List the autonomic/physical features of a panic attack.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Palpitations, tachycardia, sweating, trembling, chest pain/tightness, shortness of breath, a choking sensation, nausea, dizziness, tingling/paraesthesia, and chills/hot flushes.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: List the psychological features of a panic attack.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.back: Fear of dying, fear of losing control/'going mad', and derealisation/depersonalisation; the attacks are self-limiting (minutes) but terrifying, and patients often believe they are having a heart attack.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.front: Describe the 'fear of fear' cycle in panic disorder.
